cards.back: Existing in thought or as an idea but not having a physical or concrete existence. "The concept of justice is rather abstract." Common collocations: abstract concept, abstract idea, abstract thinking.
To succeed in achieving something, especially after a lot of effort. "She worked hard to attain her goal of becoming a doctor." Common collocations: attain goals, attain success, attain knowledge.
The majority or main part of something; large size or quantity. "The bulk of the population lives in urban areas." Common collocations: bulk of, in bulk, bulk purchase.
To stop or come to an end. "The company will cease operations next month." Common collocations: cease to exist, cease fire, cease operations.
To direct something into a particular course or use. "She channeled her energy into her studies." Common collocations: channel resources, channel efforts, communication channel.
Relating to ordinary citizens and their concerns, or polite and formal. "Civil society plays an important role in democracy." Common collocations: civil rights, civil society, civil servant.
To happen at the same time or to be in agreement. "The meeting coincides with my vacation." Common collocations: coincide with, coincide exactly, opinions coincide.
To fall down or give way suddenly; to fail completely. "The building collapsed during the earthquake." Common collocations: collapse suddenly, economic collapse, collapse under pressure.
To begin or start. "The ceremony will commence at 10 a.m." Common collocations: commence operations, commence work, commence proceedings.

A raw material or primary agricultural product that can be bought and sold. "Oil is a valuable commodity in the global market." Common collocations: commodity prices, commodity market, agricultural commodity.
To collect information and arrange it in a list, report, or book. "Researchers compiled data from multiple sources." Common collocations: compile data, compile information, compile a report.
Existing or happening at the same time. "She held two concurrent jobs to pay for tuition." Common collocations: concurrent events, concurrent sessions, run concurrently.

The process of changing something from one form, purpose, or system to another. "The conversion of farmland to housing developments is controversial." Common collocations: conversion rate, energy conversion, religious conversion.
To work together with others toward a common goal. "Countries must cooperate to address climate change." Common collocations: cooperate with, cooperate fully, willing to cooperate.

To organize different elements or people to work together effectively. "The manager coordinates activities between departments." Common collocations: coordinate efforts, coordinate activities, coordinate with.
To match or be similar to something; to communicate by letters or emails. "The results correspond with our predictions." Common collocations: correspond to, correspond with, closely correspond.
Able to be believed; convincing. "She is a credible witness in the case." Common collocations: credible source, credible evidence, credible alternative.

A system of money in general use in a particular country. "The euro is the official currency of many European countries." Common collocations: foreign currency, currency exchange, currency fluctuations.
To reach a conclusion by reasoning from evidence. "From the evidence, we can deduce that he was present at the scene." Common collocations: deduce from, deduce that, logically deduce.
A lack or shortage of something essential. "Vitamin D deficiency is common in northern countries." Common collocations: vitamin deficiency, deficiency in, nutritional deficiency.

Done consciously and intentionally; to think carefully about something. "It was a deliberate attempt to mislead the public." Common collocations: deliberate action, deliberate attempt, deliberate decision.
To discover or identify the presence of something. "Scientists can detect changes in temperature using satellites." Common collocations: detect changes, detect errors, detect early.

To recognize or show what makes things different from each other. "It is important to differentiate between facts and opinions." Common collocations: differentiate between, differentiate from, clearly differentiate.
To force something or someone out of its usual place or position. "The war displaced thousands of families." Common collocations: displace people, displace workers, internally displaced.

A difference or contrast between similar things; excellence that sets something apart. "There is a clear distinction between the two theories." Common collocations: make a distinction, clear distinction, distinction between.
To give a misleading or false account of something; to pull or twist out of shape. "The media can distort the truth." Common collocations: distort facts, distort reality, distort the image.
A specific area of knowledge or activity. "Mathematics is not my domain of expertise." Common collocations: public domain, domain of, domain knowledge.
The time during which something continues. "The duration of the course is six months." Common collocations: duration of, short duration, for the duration.

To fix something firmly and deeply in a surrounding mass; to incorporate as an integral part. "The values are embedded in the culture." Common collocations: embed in, deeply embedded, embed technology.
To compel observance of or compliance with a law, rule, or obligation. "Police are responsible for enforcing traffic laws." Common collocations: enforce laws, enforce rules, strictly enforce.
A thing with distinct and independent existence. "The company operates as a separate legal entity." Common collocations: legal entity, separate entity, business entity.
Equal in value, amount, function, or meaning. "A kilometer is equivalent to 0.62 miles." Common collocations: equivalent to, equivalent value, roughly equivalent.
To publicly display something; to show a particular quality or behavior. "The museum exhibits ancient artifacts." Common collocations: exhibit signs, exhibit behavior, on exhibit.
To remove or take out, especially by effort or force; a passage taken from a text. "Scientists extract oil from plants." Common collocations: extract information, extract data, extract from.
To make an action or process easier or less difficult. "Technology can facilitate communication across distances." Common collocations: facilitate learning, facilitate discussion, facilitate access.
The way something is arranged or presented; to arrange or put into a format. "The report should follow the standard format." Common collocations: file format, format of, format a document.
A basic structure underlying a system, concept, or text. "The legal framework protects consumer rights." Common collocations: regulatory framework, theoretical framework, framework for.
To cause something to exist or develop; to produce. "Solar panels generate electricity from sunlight." Common collocations: generate income, generate ideas, generate energy.

A system in which members are ranked according to status or authority. "The company has a strict management hierarchy." Common collocations: social hierarchy, organizational hierarchy, hierarchy of needs.

A system of ideas and ideals forming the basis of economic or political theory. "Political ideology influences policy decisions." Common collocations: political ideology, dominant ideology, ideology of.
The introduction of new ideas, methods, or products. "Technological innovation drives economic growth." Common collocations: technological innovation, promote innovation, innovation in.
Of extreme force, degree, or strength. "The competition was intense." Common collocations: intense pressure, intense heat, intense debate.
To separate something from other things; to set apart. "Researchers isolated the virus in the laboratory." Common collocations: isolate from, isolate the problem, remain isolated.
To show or prove to be right or reasonable. "How can you justify spending so much money?" Common collocations: justify the cost, justify a decision, hard to justify.
Willing to respect different behavior or opinions; generous in amount. "The university promotes liberal education." Common collocations: liberal values, liberal democracy, liberal arts.
Reasoning conducted according to strict principles of validity. "The argument lacks logic and evidence." Common collocations: sound logic, defy logic, logic behind.
The great size or extent of something; importance. "They failed to grasp the magnitude of the problem." Common collocations: magnitude of, order of magnitude, sheer magnitude.

To handle or control something in a skilful manner; to control or influence unfairly. "Some politicians manipulate public opinion through misleading statements." Common collocations: manipulate data, manipulate people, easily manipulated.

To intervene between people in a dispute to bring about an agreement. "A neutral third party was asked to mediate the negotiations." Common collocations: mediate between, mediate a dispute, mediate conflict.
To move from one region or country to another; to move from one system to another. "Thousands of birds migrate south every winter." Common collocations: migrate to, migrate from, migrate data.
